rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Resistors in series add (like capacitors in parallel). Resistors in parallel combine inversely (like capacitors in series). The rules for resistors and capacitors are always opposite.  ·  The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is always less than the smallest individual resistor. Do not think of it as simply 'dividing' — the math is $R_{eq} = (R_1 R_2)/(R_1 + R_2)$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: In series, the same current flows through all resistors, but the voltage drop across each is different (proportional to its resistance). In parallel, the same voltage is across each, but current differs.  ·  When a resistor is added in parallel, the equivalent resistance decreases. When added in series, it increases. This is because parallel paths provide more conduction channels.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The equivalent resistance of resistors in series is always greater than the largest individual resistance. The equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance.  ·  In household wiring, all appliances are connected in parallel so each receives the full supply voltage and can be operated independently.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Series:** same current through all resistors. $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \ldots$. Voltage divides: $V_i = I R_i$.  ·  **Parallel:** same voltage across all resistors. $1/R_{eq} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + \ldots$. Current divides: $I_i = V/R_i$.  ·  **Why series increases resistance:** the current must pass through each resistor sequentially, so each adds its opposition to the total.
